title: Perf-canary traffic isolation options (brainstorm + decision)
content:
Context / problem
We’re standing up a production perf regression canary. It must run continuously (per model/region slice) and produce stable p95 latency + tokens/sec time series.

Key constraint: canary traffic cannot meaningfully impact customer SLOs or queue behavior. If the canary perturbs batching/scheduler decisions (or steals GPU time), the data becomes both risky and potentially misleading.

This doc is a platform brainstorm on isolation strategies. Goal is to pick something we can ship in v1 (8-week timeline) and leave a clear path to “stronger isolation” later if needed.

Non-goals
- Perfect isolation equivalent to a dedicated benchmarking lab.
- Solving all mixed-load fairness issues across the entire fleet.

Design principles
1) Safety first: canary should never be able to cause an incident.
2) Don’t distort what we measure: we want “real production stack” effects, but not at the cost of changing customer behavior.
3) Low operational overhead: no extra fleet management complexity unless we really need it.
4) Measurable guarantees: the isolation mechanism should be explainable (hard caps) vs “best effort”.

Option A — Dedicated queue within the same scheduler (separate internal queue, hard caps)
Summary
Create a distinct scheduler queue for canary requests (separate from customer queues). Enforce strict caps: max concurrent canary requests per node, max canary tokens/sec per node, and/or max KV cache footprint. The scheduler always prefers customer queues, but canary queue drains when there’s slack.

Pros
- Stronger than pure “low priority” because we can add explicit limits.
- Minimizes impact on customer tail latency (customer-first ordering).
- Implementation scoped to scheduler layer (no need to carve out an entire GPU pool).
- Good for attribution: we can tag canary queue metrics separately and enforce deterministic policies.

Cons / risks
- Still shares the same hardware and will be sensitive to background contention (which is partly the point, but it will add variance).
- Needs careful implementation to avoid pathological interactions:
  - Canary queue shouldn’t change batch composition for customer requests.
  - Canary work should not trigger kernel autotune or cache evictions that impact customers.
- If “customer-first” is too strict, canary may starve during sustained load, reducing sample size (and causing noisy metrics).

Notes
- This is very aligned with what SRE wants: “canary should be impossible to page us by causing customer pain.”
- Needs a defined fairness policy for the canary queue: e.g., run only when customer queue depth < threshold OR allocate a tiny guaranteed slice.

Option B — Low-priority request class (single queue, priority bit)
Summary
Mark canary requests as low priority so they are de-prioritized relative to customer requests. Keep all requests in the same queue, but assign a priority score.

Pros
- Simplest to implement.
- Least structural change (no new queue objects, fewer metrics changes).
- Could be enough if combined with strict rate limits at the canary runner.

Cons / risks
- Harder to reason about; priority systems often have edge cases.
- Can still distort batch composition and queue dynamics because low-priority requests are physically present in the same batching flow.
- Without hard caps, low-priority traffic can still consume GPU cycles under some conditions (e.g., when batching tries to “fill” batches).
- Debugging is harder: “why was canary running right now?” can turn into heuristics archaeology.

Notes
- If we do this, we likely still want a per-node hard cap, which basically turns it into Option A anyway.

Option C — Dedicated GPU pool / node pool for canary
Summary
Stand up a small canary-only pool per region (and possibly per GPU SKU). Canary runner routes only to this pool.

Pros
- Strongest isolation from customer queues (near-zero risk of customer impact).
- Canary measurements become much more stable (no mixed load contention).
- Easier “known-good baseline” behavior since the environment is more controlled.

Cons / risks
- Expensive: reserving GPU capacity that’s mostly idle.
- Operational overhead:
  - Separate autoscaling rules.
  - Separate model loading / cache warmups.
  - Separate health checks and release orchestration.
- Less representative of real production fleet behavior, which is one of the core reasons we’re doing a prod canary.
- Fleet heterogeneity becomes harder: do we need one canary pool per GPU SKU to avoid mixing? (likely yes).

Notes
- This is a good v2 lever if we find the canary too noisy under Option A.

Option D — Time-sliced execution windows (run canary only in low-traffic periods)
Summary
Schedule canary runs during pre-defined low-traffic hours and pause during peak.

Pros
- Reduces risk of impact during peak.
- Potentially reduces variance if the system is otherwise quiet.

Cons / risks
- Defeats the purpose of continuous detection (we’ll miss regressions that only show under peak conditions).
- Introduces biased data: low-traffic performance may look “fine” while peak degrades.
- Operational complexity around global regions/time zones.

Option E — Shadow-mode / sampling from real traffic
Summary
Attach instrumentation to a sampled subset of real customer requests (or duplicate the request to a “shadow” execution path).

Pros
- Most representative.
- Avoids synthetic prompts concerns.

Cons / risks
- This is not safe/acceptable for v1:
  - Duplicating real traffic doubles compute cost.
  - Touches customer data/PII considerations.
  - Makes isolation harder: the canary is no longer explicitly bounded.

Decision (v1)
We will implement a “canary-safe request class” that maps to a dedicated scheduler queue with strict caps (Option A), plus runner-side rate limits.

Working name: canary-safe class.

Rationale
- Better safety guarantees than simple priority tagging.
- Much less cost/overhead than dedicated GPU pools.
- Gives us explicit levers to control/measure impact: concurrency caps, tokens/sec caps, and clear per-queue metrics.

Key requirements for the chosen approach
1) Hard limits (must-have)
- Max concurrent canary requests per node (initial proposal: 1).
- Max in-flight canary tokens per node (initial: small; exact number TBD after first week of data).
- Optional: limit canary KV cache footprint (e.g., max cached tokens attributed to canary).

2) Customer-first behavior (must-have)
- Customer requests should always preempt canary scheduling.
- Canary should not “fill” batches for customer requests.

3) Canary starvation protection (nice-to-have)
- If a node is continuously busy, canary may never run. That’s acceptable short-term if we have enough capacity across the region, but we need to watch sample size.
- Potential compromise: allow canary to run at a minimal trickle even when busy (e.g., 1 request every N minutes), but only if impact is proven negligible.

4) Isolation from side effects (must-have)
- Kernel autotune / compilation artifacts must not be triggered by canary in a way that impacts customers.
  - If there are “warmup” steps required, do them using the same canary-safe class and ensure they obey caps.
- Canary metrics/logging overhead should be gated behind the canary tag.

5) Observability (must-have)
- Every canary request must be tagged (source=perf-canary) and include runtime_build, scheduler_mode, gpu_sku, region.
- Scheduler metrics should expose per-queue:
  - queue_depth
  - dequeue latency
  - run time
  - dropped/throttled counts due to caps

Implementation sketch (for alignment)
- Canary runner:
  - Enforces global RPS/token budget per region.
  - Uses separate auth identity / client to ensure it cannot bypass quotas.
- Runtime gateway / router:
  - Sets request_class=CANARY_SAFE based on auth identity or explicit header allowed only for the canary service.
- Scheduler:
  - Creates separate internal queue for CANARY_SAFE.
  - Applies strict caps.
  - Customer queues have strict precedence.

Open questions
- Do we need caps at multiple levels (global region cap + per-node cap)? Likely yes.
- Can canary requests share KV cache with customer traffic? Probably “no” by default; shared cache makes side effects hard to reason about.
- What’s the right starvation policy (if any)? Let’s measure first.
- Do we need to pin scheduler mode for canary to reduce variance? (likely yes; see ENG-2854)

Risks / mitigation
- Risk: Canary starves under real load → Mitigation: run across multiple nodes/regions; monitor sample size and add minimal guaranteed trickle if safe.
- Risk: Canary impacts customer batching → Mitigation: prohibit cross-queue batching; validate with A/B in a single region before expanding.
- Risk: Implementation complexity delays v1 → Mitigation: keep queue model minimal; treat dedicated GPU pool as v2.

Next steps
- Align on cap defaults with SRE (Sean, Tomáš) and Runtime (Noah).
- Implement canary-safe class + queue in runtime (tracked in PR: GitHub:redwood/pr_39203).
- Add metrics for throttling/drops so we can prove isolation.
- Update canary design doc and rollout checklist to reflect this decision.

Change log
- 2026-01-09: initial brainstorm draft (Sofia)
- 2026-01-14: added hard-cap requirements + starvation notes after SRE review
- 2026-01-21: updated decision to “dedicated queue + canary-safe class” to match runtime implementation direction
